summary:
Spaceflight medical teams face a critical telemetry bottleneck: astronaut vitals, dosimeters, and habitat sensors are scattered across disconnected tabular logs and ground-related protocols. During deep-space communication delays, crews cannot wait on Earth to cross-check spreadsheets for silent hazards.

A²U.R.A. collates real-time biometric wearables, cabin environmental sensors, cognitive tests, and behavioral cues into a single offline-ready onboard database. It renders an interactive 3D digital twin of the astronaut, featuring color-coded anatomical "auras" and immediate countermeasure guidance.
details:
In 2019, a NASA astronaut aboard the International Space Station became the first person in history to be diagnosed with and treated for a deep vein thrombosis (blood clot) in space, discovered completely by accident during a routine research study. If the clot had not been discovered in time, it could have broken loose and travelled to the lungs, which would have been fatal. This is just one of the many health risks astronauts experience in space. Due to the isolated nature of space travel, astronauts do not have easy access to healthcare and medicine, meaning underlying health complications that seem simple on Earth can prove fatal in the long run.

Figure 1. Nominal operational view of A²U.R.A. (AURA-1 · live demo) displaying the 3D astronaut digital twin alongside live biometric vitals (70 bpm HR, 37.0 °C Core Temp, 225 ms PVT+) and cabin environmental telemetry.

How We Addressed This Challenge

A²U.R.A. bridges the gap between raw spaceflight telemetry and rapid clinical action. Rather than forcing crew members or flight surgeons to manually parse separate monitors, our platform maps anomalies directly onto affected anatomical regions (Brain, Heart, Gastrointestinal Tract, or Full Body) using a two-tier color taxonomy:

Severity Action Indicators:

  • Red: Immediate Threshold Breach / Action ASAP.
  • Yellow: Caution / Elevated Parameters.

Parameter-Specific Environmental Indicators:

  • Blue: Lowered Temperatures / Cold Stress.
  • Green: Ionizing Radiation Exposure.
  • Gray: Subpar Air Quality / CO.

When multiple hazards occur simultaneously, a 7-tier priority hierarchy ranks top-banner alerts by time-to-incapacitation, prioritizing acute toxic gas and solar particle storms first while retaining secondary anatomical highlights on the 3D mesh.

Figure 2. Multi-hazard critical escalation showing simultaneous Cabin cold · critical (15.4 °C) and Acute absorbed dose / GI risk · critical alerts mapped onto the 3D astronaut with prioritized "What to do next" crew instructions.

How It Works

A²U.R.A. aggregates four native International Space Station (ISS) telemetry streams into a multi-layered correlation engine:

1. Environmental & Habitat Telemetry (ISS ECLSS)

Tracks ionizing radiation (TEPC/HERA/DOSTEL), carbon monoxide (CSA-CP), and cabin duct temperatures against NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2 and NASA JSC-20584 limits (10 ppm CO early warning; 425 ppm 1-hour acute limit; 1.0 Gy acute GI radiation threshold).

2. Physiological & Thermal Biometrics

Monitors continuous wrist-wearable HRV (RMSSD), heart rate trends, sleep architecture, and Thermolab core body temperature (36.5°C–37.5°C optimal; ≥ 39.0°C critical hyperthermia).

3. Ambient Computer Vision & Cognitive Vigilance (NASA PVT+)

Combines 5-minute Psychomotor Vigilance Test reaction times (> 250 ms warning; > 350 ms critical) with non-invasive oculomotor (PERCLOS) and facial effect analysis.

4. Multi-Modal Mental Health Index (MHI)

Synthesizes biometrics, visual affect, and encrypted daily journal NLP sentiment:

MHI = w1 * (Biometrics) + w2 * (Visual/Affect) + w3 * (Journal Sentiment) 

If an astronaut reports "I'm fine" while HRV drops and PVT+ slows, A²U.R.A. triggers a Cross-Validation Discrepancy Alert.

Figure 4. Live telemetry readout drawer (Acute absorbed dose, Cumulative effective dose, PVT+ lapses, HRV, CO, CO₂, Cabin/Core temp) alongside batch mission crew profiles (AST-001 through AST-005 · CSV demo).

Main Insights

Testing A²U.R.A. using real ISS radiation data and five simulated astronaut scenarios revealed four important insights:

  • Recognizing Unusual Radiation Levels: By studying actual radiation records from the ISS, A²U.R.A. established a baseline for normal exposure. This helps the system recognize when radiation levels begin to rise beyond expected conditions.
  • Identifying the Source of Health Risks: A²U.R.A. compares astronaut health readings with cabin conditions to help distinguish whether unusual symptoms may be caused by the environment or the astronaut's physical condition.
  • Detecting Fatigue Before Astronauts Notice It: The system can identify early signs of fatigue through changes in heart rate variability and reaction time, even when astronauts report feeling fine.
  • Prioritizing Emergencies: When several health and environmental risks occur at once, A²U.R.A. ranks alerts according to urgency, helping astronauts recognize which threats require immediate attention instead of overwhelming them with multiple warnings.

Key Insights & Validation Table

Figure 5. Empirical ISS accumulated radiation curve (NASA OSDR RR-1 EDA, Mission Days 1–39) used as A²U.R.A.'s baseline anomaly detection slope.

Impact

In isolated, confined, and extreme (ICE) environments such as Artemis lunar habitats or Mars transit vehicles, communication lags make real-time Earth triage impossible.

A²U.R.A. empowers crews with offline-capable, privacy-first medical autonomy by converting raw video and journal feeds locally into anonymized metadata vectors. This approach supports earlier hazard detection, reduces psychological stigma, and helps prevent human error during high-risk EVA, docking, and robotics operations.

How We Developed This Project

Frontend & 3D Visualization

Built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Three.js to render the interactive 3D astronaut digital twin, real-time telemetry charts, and dynamic anatomical aura shaders.

Data Modeling & AI Synthesis

Integrated Google Gemini API for structured behavioral and journal parsing, Python (Pyplot) for orbital radiation curve modeling, and Google Stitch, Claude Code, and Codex for rapid UI/UX prototyping and code verification.

NASA Data & Standards

Grounded in NASA OSDR RR-1 EDA, OSD-1014, OSD-575, NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2, NASA JSC-20584, NASA PVT+, and OCHMO spaceflight technical briefs.
